name: Bacopa (Bacopa monnieri)
short: Adverse-event reports: heart attack with moclobemide (chart review); suspected cholinergic toxicity with cevimeline (case report). Older adults: gut upset in 1 trial; 9 events vs 10 on placebo in 1.
text: Two randomised, placebo-controlled 12-week trials of Bacopa in older adults gave different pictures: in 98 healthy people over 55 (the abstract does not state the route), Bacopa caused gastrointestinal side effects (increased stool frequency, abdominal cramps and nausea) compared with placebo, while in 54 people aged 65 or over taking an extract by mouth there were few adverse events, mainly stomach upset (9 with Bacopa, 10 with placebo; the abstract reports no statistical test of this difference). A systematic review of five studies in children and adolescents found that 2.3% of all participants reported mild side effects (safety data were well reported in 80% of the studies). Reports of harm alongside medicines come from a chart review and a case report rather than trials: a retrospective review of 1,816 adverse-event reports identified 30 reports judged to show a high probability of a causal interaction between an adaptogen and an antidepressant, and for Bacopa monnieri these were back pain and excessive sweating with agomelatine and a myocardial infarction (heart attack) with moclobemide; the abstract does not say how many reports involved Bacopa, and the authors point to inhibition of CYP enzymes and p-glycoprotein as possible mechanisms. A case report describes a 58-year-old woman taking cevimeline for Sjögren's syndrome who developed excessive sweating, malaise, nausea and a fast heart rate, described as suspected cholinergic toxicity, after taking a supplement containing Bacopa monnieri and phosphatidylserine; she improved with fluids after the supplement was stopped. A 2025 narrative review describes Bacopa as generally non-toxic with no serious side effects reported, but says interactions with certain medications and contraindications such as hyperthyroidism should be considered, and that more research on safety is needed, especially for pregnant and breastfeeding women.
